summary.title: Build It Yourself
summary.one_liner: Armin Ronacher argues for fewer dependencies, showing how small crates pull in large transitive graphs and why writing a small function yourself can be the lower-maintenance choice.
keywords: write it yourself instead of library
takeaways: Small crates such as terminal_size can add several transitive crates and trigger long compile chains for trivial functionality.
Stable code that works can avoid the maintenance treadmill of constant updates, audits, and dependabot pull requests.
Writing a small, stable function yourself is often less maintenance than tracking an upstream dependency, though it is more work up front.
Large dependency graphs deserve scrutiny, but important libraries solving hard problems (e.g. tokio, HTTP/QUIC) are still worth using.
Projects like minijinja show a minimal-dependency approach; the author plans to trim dependencies in his own projects.
summary.summary: This opinion essay by Armin Ronacher critiques dependency churn in ecosystems like Rust and JavaScript. He uses examples such as terminal_size, Tokio, Rocket, MiniJinja, and the sha1 crate to show how small libraries can pull in many transitive crates and frequent updates. He argues that developers should value minimal dependencies and self-written small functions, while acknowledging that major libraries for hard problems remain justified. The piece is a personal perspective rather than a how-to, and it is not a tutorial.
